h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: Near-divergent learning rates are partly stabilized by lower-noise larger-batch gradients, while update count is no longer the bottleneck.
With Adam a fixed per-parameter step moves wider nets' outputs further, so width compensates for too-small learning rates.
Narrow nets are already capacity-limited and do not overfit, so extra weight shrinkage pushes them into underfitting more than wide nets.
Gradient and update magnitudes compound across layers, so deeper ReLU stacks diverge or die more readily at large learning rates.
Small batches supply many updates within 243 epochs, letting deeper nets actually realize their extra capacity.
Single-hidden-layer nets get capacity only from width, whereas deeper nets already have enough representational power.
Stacking narrow ReLU layers creates information bottlenecks and dead units that make the extra layer harmful rather than helpful.
Large batches give few, low-noise updates per epoch, so a larger step size is needed to converge within the budget.
Heavy L2 forces the net into an underfit regime where extra units are shrunk toward zero and add little, unlike at mild regularization where width helps.
Tiny batches give many noisy updates, so lowering the learning rate reduces noise at little cost in convergence.
